title: Drug Screens: The Screen Accuses, the Mass Spec Decides
summary: See why a positive immunoassay drug screen is only presumptive, how confirmation by chromatography and mass spectrometry works, and how labs judge whether a urine specimen is valid, dilute or substituted.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 24 Hit 1 (core: one immunoassay cannot confirm another; chain of custody), Hit 2 (GC-MS / LC-MS/MS as confirmation tools), Trap 2 (repeat immunoassay), Trap 3 (dilute specimen) and the Figure 24 anchor. Checked against 49 CFR Part 40, Argoff 2018 and Wissenbach & Steuer 2023. Trap 3 numbers differ from the DOT laboratory criteria — see register flags rv-dilute-criteria and rv-temp-substituted. Pending: TLC as a confirmation method; GC-MS vs LC-MS/MS by volatility/derivatization.

objectives: Explain why a screening immunoassay result is presumptive and why a second immunoassay cannot confirm it.
Describe confirmation as an independent procedure on a separate aliquot using chromatography with mass spectrometry.
Apply specimen-validity criteria (temperature, creatinine, specific gravity) and explain chain of custody.

scenes.title: A positive screen — so test it again?
scenes.altText: A urine cup labelled “Urine”. A screening immunoassay card turns “Opiates: POSITIVE”. Someone proposes “Repeat the same immunoassay to confirm”; a second identical card also turns positive, and a question mark asks whether that proves anything.

cues.text: A workplace urine sample screens positive for opiates on an immunoassay.
Someone suggests running the same kind of immunoassay again to confirm it. It comes back positive again.
Two positives. But does the second one prove anything the first one didn’t?

scenes.title: Normal: what a screening immunoassay really says
scenes.altText: An antibody recognises a drug by shape. A look-alike molecule fits the same antibody, so the screen lights up anyway (cross-reactivity → false positive). A cut-off line splits results: below it the specimen is reported negative; at or above it the result is only presumptive and goes on to confirmation.

cues.text: A screening immunoassay uses antibodies that recognise a drug by its shape. It is fast, cheap and easy to automate.
But a different molecule with a similar shape can fit the same antibody. That is cross-reactivity, and it causes false positives. Some drugs in a class are also missed.
So the screen is compared with a cut-off. Below the cut-off, the specimen can be reported negative.
At or above the cut-off, the result is only presumptive. It is a reason to test further, not an answer.

scenes.title: What changes: confirmation by an independent method
scenes.altText: A fresh aliquot is poured from the original specimen. It flows into a chromatography column, where bands separate by time; each band then enters a mass spectrometer box that reads its mass fingerprint and gives a concentration. A side panel shows that the screening and confirmation cut-offs differ (example: marijuana metabolite screen 50 ng/mL, confirmation 15 ng/mL).

cues.text: Confirmation is a second, different analytical procedure, run on a separate aliquot of the original specimen.
First, chromatography separates the molecules, so look-alikes come off at different times.
Then mass spectrometry identifies each one by its mass fingerprint and measures how much is there. Gas or liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry are the usual tools.
The two steps use different cut-offs. In US federal workplace testing, the marijuana metabolite screen cut-off is 50 nanograms per millilitre, but the confirmation cut-off is 15.

scenes.title: In the lab: is the specimen valid?
scenes.altText: A checklist builds. Temperature at collection: read within 4 minutes, acceptable 32–38 °C (90–100 °F); out of range means an immediate new collection under direct observation. Creatinine on every specimen; specific gravity if creatinine is below 20 mg/dL. Two result cards: Dilute (creatinine ≥ 2 and < 20 mg/dL with SG > 1.0010 and < 1.0030) and Substituted (creatinine < 2 mg/dL with SG ≤ 1.0010 or ≥ 1.0200). A chain-of-custody form slides along the bottom with signatures.

cues.text: Before a result can be trusted, so must the specimen. At collection, temperature is read within four minutes. The acceptable range is 32 to 38 degrees Celsius.
If it’s out of range, the collector immediately starts a new collection under direct observation.
In the lab, creatinine is measured on every specimen. Specific gravity is added when creatinine is below 20 milligrams per decilitre.

Under US federal rules, a dilute specimen has creatinine from 2 up to just under 20, and specific gravity just above 1.001 but below 1.003. Lower than that — creatinine under 2 with an extreme specific gravity — means substituted: that is not human urine.
And every hand-off, from collection to result, is signed and documented. That record is the chain of custody.

props.label: Out of range → new observed collection
Chain of custody: collector → courier → lab ✍

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Repeat immunoassay (or a different immunoassay) confirms” is crossed out → “Confirm with an independent method: chromatography + mass spectrometry.” Trap card: “Dilute specimen, drug not detected = clean negative” is crossed out → “Report it as dilute; a low concentration may sit under the cut-off.” Trap card: “Hot or cold cup = substituted” is crossed out → “Temperature is a collection check that triggers an observed recollection.”

cues.text: Trap one: a repeat immunoassay, or a different immunoassay, is not confirmation. Both rely on antibody binding. Confirmation needs an independent method, such as chromatography with mass spectrometry.
Trap two: a dilute specimen with no drug detected is not simply clean. Dilution can push a drug under the cut-off, so it is reported as dilute.
Trap three: a cup outside the temperature range isn’t a lab result of “substituted.” It’s a collection check that triggers a new, observed collection.

props.title: ✗ “Dilute + not detected = clean negative.”
lines: ✓ Reported as dilute — drug may sit under the cut-off

scenes.title: The screen accuses, the mass spec decides
scenes.altText: Memory aid: a magnifying-glass token “Screen accuses” and a gavel token “Mass spec decides”, with a reminder that the specimen itself must be valid. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the screen accuses, the mass spec decides — and only if the specimen itself is valid.

Where it breaks: a medical review officer, not the lab, interprets a confirmed positive, and a prescription can explain it. Some labs now screen by mass spectrometry. And the exact cut-offs belong to the program — these numbers are US federal workplace rules.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Immunoassay screen = presumptive”, “Confirm on a new aliquot by chromatography + MS”, “Check validity: temperature, creatinine, SG, chain of custody”.

cues.text: A positive immunoassay screen is only presumptive: confirm it on a separate aliquot by an independent method such as chromatography with mass spectrometry, and check that the specimen is valid before trusting any result.

props.label: Confirm on a new aliquot by chromatography + MS
Check validity: temperature, creatinine, SG, custody

explanation.what: Plain language: a drug screen is a quick antibody test that can be fooled by look-alike molecules, so a positive screen must be checked by a different, more specific method. Scientific terms: immunoassay screens are presumptive because of antibody cross-reactivity; confirmatory testing is a second analytical procedure, on a different aliquot of the original specimen, that identifies and quantifies the drug — typically GC-MS or LC-MS(/MS).
explanation.why: Two immunoassays share the same weakness (antibody recognition by shape), so agreement between them does not rule out cross-reactivity. Chromatography separates compounds and mass spectrometry identifies them by mass, which is independent of antibody binding.
explanation.measure: Screen against a cut-off (below = negative; at/above = presumptive); confirm by chromatography–MS with its own cut-off (US DOT example: marijuana metabolite 50 ng/mL screen, 15 ng/mL confirmation). Validity (US DOT, 49 CFR Part 40): temperature 32–38 °C within 4 minutes at collection, out of range → immediate observed recollection; creatinine on every specimen, SG if creatinine < 20 mg/dL; dilute = creatinine ≥ 2 and < 20 mg/dL with SG > 1.0010 and < 1.0030; substituted = creatinine < 2 mg/dL with SG ≤ 1.0010 or ≥ 1.0200. Chain of custody documents every hand-off.
explanation.differs: Presumptive (immunoassay) vs definitive (chromatography–MS) testing; dilute (still human urine, diluted) vs substituted (not consistent with human urine); collection-site checks (temperature) vs laboratory validity tests (creatinine, SG, pH, oxidants).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: “repeat EMIT/FPIA to confirm” (wrong), GC-MS as the classic confirmation method, dilute vs substituted creatinine/SG criteria, and chain of custody.

comparisons.title: Screen vs confirmation
comparisons.distinguisher: Independent principle: separation plus mass identification, not antibody binding.

comparisons.title: Dilute vs substituted (US DOT)
comparisons.distinguisher: Creatinine below 2 mg/dL with an extreme SG is not consistent with human urine.

mnemonic.text: The screen accuses, the mass spec decides — if the specimen is valid.
mnemonic.explanation: An immunoassay positive is an accusation (presumptive); chromatography–mass spectrometry on a separate aliquot decides; validity checks make sure the specimen is real urine from the donor.
mnemonic.limitation: A confirmed positive still goes to medical review (a prescription can explain it); some labs screen by MS; cut-offs and validity rules are program-specific (the numbers shown are US federal workplace rules).

analogyLimitations: Antibody, column and band tokens are schematic.
Validity criteria shown are the US DOT laboratory rules; clinical and other national programs may use different flags.
takeaway: A positive immunoassay screen is only presumptive: confirm it on a separate aliquot by an independent method such as chromatography with mass spectrometry, and check that the specimen is valid before trusting any result.

questions.stem: An EMIT urine screen is positive for opiates. Which follow-up counts as confirmation?

options.text: GC-MS or LC-MS/MS on a separate aliquot of the original specimen
options.rationale: Correct. Confirmation is an independent analytical procedure, on a different aliquot, that identifies and quantifies the drug.

options.text: Repeating the EMIT on the same specimen
options.rationale: Incorrect. Repeating the same immunoassay only reproduces the same cross-reactivity.
Incorrect. FPIA is also an immunoassay, so it is not an independent principle.

options.text: Collecting a new specimen and repeating the screen
options.rationale: Incorrect. A second screen is still presumptive and breaks the link to the original specimen.

questions.stem: Under US DOT laboratory criteria, a urine specimen has creatinine 12 mg/dL and specific gravity 1.0020. How is it classified?

options.rationale: Correct. Creatinine ≥ 2 and < 20 mg/dL with SG > 1.0010 and < 1.0030 meets the dilute criteria.
Incorrect. Substituted requires creatinine < 2 mg/dL with SG ≤ 1.0010 or ≥ 1.0200.
Incorrect. The values meet dilute criteria, which must be reported.
Incorrect. Adulteration is shown by an added substance or abnormal pH, not by creatinine and SG alone.

questions.stem: Within four minutes of collection, a urine cup reads 30 °C (86 °F). What should happen?

options.text: Note it and immediately collect a new specimen under direct observation
options.rationale: Correct. In US DOT collections, an out-of-range temperature triggers an immediate new collection under direct observation; both specimens are sent.
Incorrect. “Substituted” is a laboratory result based on creatinine and specific gravity, not on temperature.

options.text: Discard the cup and send the donor home
options.rationale: Incorrect. The original specimen is still processed, alongside the observed one.

options.text: Warm the cup to 35 °C and send it to the lab
options.rationale: Incorrect. That would falsify the specimen record.

claims.text: Immunoassay screens are presumptive: cross-reactivity causes false positives; cut-offs and cross-reactivity cause false negatives.
Confirmation is a second analytical procedure on a different aliquot that identifies and quantifies the drug, typically GC-MS or LC-MS(/MS); a second immunoassay is not independent.
US DOT marijuana metabolite cut-offs: 50 ng/mL screen, 15 ng/mL confirmation.
US DOT: temperature 32–38 °C within 4 min (out of range → observed recollection); creatinine every specimen, SG if < 20 mg/dL; dilute and substituted criteria.
Chain of custody documents specimen handling from collection to result.
TLC is an acceptable independent confirmation method for EMIT.

claims.text: GC-MS suits volatile analytes; LC-MS/MS handles polar, thermolabile, nonvolatile molecules without derivatization.
